meta.title: Cuban Elections
sources: Wikipedia: Cuban general, parliamentary and presidential election articles 1901-2023 (results tables and infoboxes)

presEras.label: Palma and the first republic
presEras.blurb: Tomás Estrada Palma won Cuba's first presidential election unopposed after his only rival withdrew citing irregularities, and won a second term in 1905 in a vote a US peace commission later found so tainted by fraud that it suspended the Congress the election had also produced.

presEras.label: A fraudulent decade, then Machado
presEras.blurb: Real multi-candidate contests decided the presidency through the 1920s, but 1920's result was accepted only after the US ambassador substantiated Liberal fraud accusations against it, and 1924's, which made Gerardo Machado president, was itself deemed fraudulent before he abolished the one-term pledge he had campaigned on. His 1928 re-election had no other candidate on the ballot at all, and the opposition was repressed.

presEras.label: The competitive years
presEras.blurb: Cuba's most consistently competitive presidential elections, run under the new 1940 constitution, with genuine multi-candidate fields each time and no fraud recorded in the source. 1948's four-way race was the widest field the republic's presidency ever saw.

presEras.label: Batista's return
presEras.blurb: Fulgencio Batista seized power in a 1952 coup that pre-empted that year's scheduled election, then won the 1954 vote after the main opposition candidate withdrew before polling day. His chosen successor won the 1958 election against a public rebel boycott call and never took office: the Cuban Revolution triumphed nine weeks after the vote.

legEras.label: The young republic
legEras.blurb: Cuba's first House of Representatives was elected under American oversight after the 1898 war, and the 1905 election that followed handed the Moderate Party 31 of the House's 32 seats amid an electoral roll a US commission called inflated by 150,000 names. A peace commission sent by Theodore Roosevelt found the 1905 vote so tainted by fraud that it suspended Congress outright the following year.

legEras.label: Fraud, coalitions and a one-party sham
legEras.blurb: Multi-party coalitions filled the House through the 1920s, but the period's two biggest results carry a shadow: the Liberal Party's 1920 accusation of fraud against the ruling Conservatives was substantiated by the US ambassador and forced new elections in four provinces, and the 1924 vote that made Gerardo Machado's coalition the largest in the House was itself deemed fraudulent before he turned the presidency into a dictatorship. No House was elected in 1928 at all; that year's article covers only Machado's unopposed re-election.

legEras.label: The 1940 constitution's decade
legEras.blurb: Women voted for the first time in 1936 and seven were elected to the House that year, and the 1940 constitution that followed brought Cuba's most genuinely competitive stretch of multi-party elections, ending with a four-party presidential field in 1948. Batista's 1952 coup pre-empted the next scheduled vote; 1954's contest went ahead with the main opposition candidate withdrawing before polling day, and 1958's, held against a public rebel boycott call, elected a House and a president who never took office once the revolution triumphed that January.

legEras.label: The National Assembly of People's Power
legEras.blurb: Cuba's post-revolutionary legislature was chosen indirectly through municipal assemblies for its first three elections, 1976 to 1986, before a 1992 electoral law moved to direct election in 1993. Every election since has offered one list, the Communist Party of Cuba and its affiliated mass organisations, and the declared result has always equalled the number of seats: the National Assembly's own size.

presidential.summary: Tomás Estrada Palma won with 158,116 votes. Turnout 63.5%.
presidential.caveat: The only other candidate, Bartolomé Masó, withdrew from the election citing irregularities, though he still received 55,000 votes.

presidential.summary: Tomás Estrada Palma won with 306,874 votes.
presidential.caveat: A US peace commission later found the vote so tainted by fraud that it suspended the Congress the election had also produced.

presidential.summary: José Miguel Gómez won with 60.70% against Mario García Menocal on 39.30%.
Mario García Menocal won with 195,504 votes.
Mario García Menocal was re-elected over Alfredo Zayas; the source records no vote count for the contest.
presidential.caveat: The article names Mario García Menocal's re-election over Alfredo Zayas but records no vote count or turnout for this contest.

presidential.summary: Alfredo Zayas y Alfonso won with 148,278 votes.
presidential.caveat: The Liberal Party accused the winning candidate and his Conservatives of election fraud, and the US ambassador to Cuba substantiated it.
The election was deemed to be fraudulent, and the winner, Gerardo Machado, established a dictatorship that lasted until his overthrow in 1933.

presidential.summary: Only one candidate was nominated, so no vote was held.
presidential.caveat: Machado ran as the only candidate after abandoning his one-term pledge, and the opposition was repressed.

presidential.summary: Miguel Mariano Gómez won with 343,289 votes.
Carlos Prío Socarrás won with 905,198 votes.

presidential.caveat: The main opposition candidate, Ramón Grau, withdrew his candidacy before election day, after Batista's 1952 coup pre-empted the vote originally scheduled that year.

presidential.summary: Andrés Rivero Agüero won with 70.40% against Carlos Márquez Sterling on 15.69%.
presidential.caveat: Rebels publicly called for an election boycott before the vote, and the declared winner was unable to take office once the Cuban Revolution triumphed nine weeks later.

legislative.summary: PNC finished first with 27 of 63 seats. Turnout 63.5%. Tomás Estrada Palma took office.
Moderate Party finished first with 31 of 32 seats. Tomás Estrada Palma stayed in office.
legislative.caveat: A US peace commission later found the vote so tainted by fraud that it suspended the Congress the election had produced; a Cuban minister told American commissioners it was impossible to hold an election in Cuba without fraud.

legislative.summary: Liberal Coalition finished first with 49 of 83 seats. José Miguel Gómez replaced Tomás Estrada Palma.
Liberal Party of Cuba finished first with 24 of 50 seats. Mario García Menocal replaced José Miguel Gómez.
National Conservative Party finished first with 27 of 60 seats. Mario García Menocal stayed in office.
Liberal Party of Cuba finished first with 28 of 59 seats. Alfredo Zayas y Alfonso replaced Mario García Menocal.
legislative.caveat: The Liberal Party accused the ruling coalition of election fraud, the US ambassador substantiated it, and new elections were held in four provinces as a result.

legislative.summary: Liberal Party of Cuba finished first with 27 of 53 seats. Gerardo Machado replaced Alfredo Zayas y Alfonso.
legislative.caveat: The election was deemed to be fraudulent, and the winning coalition's leader, Gerardo Machado, established a dictatorship that lasted until his overthrow in 1933.

legislative.summary: Democratic National Association finished first with 70 of 162 seats. Miguel Mariano Gómez replaced José Agripino Barnet.
Partido Auténtico finished first with 34 of 156 seats. Fulgencio Batista replaced Federico Laredo Brú.
Partido Auténtico finished first with 19 of 70 seats. Ramón Grau replaced Fulgencio Batista.
Partido Auténtico finished first with 29 of 70 seats. Carlos Prío Socarrás replaced Ramón Grau.
Progressive Action Party finished first with 60 of 130 seats. Fulgencio Batista stayed in office.
legislative.caveat: Held after Fulgencio Batista's 1952 coup pre-empted the scheduled election, with the main opposition candidate withdrawing his own candidacy before polling day.

legislative.summary: Progressive Action Party finished first with 65 of 166 seats. Andrés Rivero Agüero replaced Fulgencio Batista.
legislative.caveat: Rebels publicly called for an election boycott before the vote, and the winner and every other elected official were unable to take office once the Cuban Revolution triumphed weeks later.

legislative.summary: PCC finished first with 489 of 489 seats. Fidel Castro stayed in office.
legislative.caveat: The Communist Party of Cuba and its affiliated mass organisations are the only names on the ballot; the declared result has equalled the National Assembly's own seat total at every election since 1993, and the first three, 1976 to 1986, were chosen indirectly through municipal assemblies with no results table on file at all.
